PLAN REVIEW RETURNED BLOCK WITH TWO FINDINGS. BOTH ACCEPTED — one was a factual error of mine, and I
verified it in source before conceding rather than deferring to the reviewer.

FINDING 1 (impact 0.8) — the plan contradicted ITSELF on the headroom threshold. Approach said assert
`< 700` "same as the existing seam tests"; Testing said assert `< 800` now and let the extraction
tickets tighten. Both were mine, in the same document. RESOLVED IN FAVOUR OF STAGING, because the
staged form is the only one that lands: the two files this guard covers are ABOVE 700 TODAY
(workflow_ops.py 794, config.py 793), so a `< 700` assertion lands RED. This ticket now asserts
`< 800` — still a real guard, it catches the next commit that would breach the hard cap — and each
sibling EXTRACTION ticket tightens its own file to `< 700` in the same change that creates the
headroom. Every ticket stays independently landable. `< 700` remains the POLICY number, with its
calibration retained (median per-commit delta ~+10, mean ~+18, p90 ~+45, worst +185 on f373cf4a6e).

FINDING 2 (impact 1.0) — I ASSERTED A STALE DOCSTRING THAT IS NOT STALE. My Scope listed
`plan_review_recovery.py:8` as needing a stale-docstring correction. VERIFIED IN SOURCE: that
docstring says three of the five finalize_verdict call sites "live in THIS CLUSTER", and there are
exactly three in that file — `:223`, `:297`, `:336`. It is ACCURATE. I had mentally attributed
test_gate_dispatch_seam.py's wording to it.
The genuinely stale text is test_gate_dispatch_seam.py's own ASSERTION MESSAGE, which asserts on
`gate_dispatch.py` while describing "its three finalize_verdict call sites" — gate_dispatch now holds
ZERO of them. (Its docstring at :3-5 reads as historical narration of the pre-split state, so it is
defensible; the assertion message is not.) Scope and file_impact corrected: plan_review_recovery.py
REMOVED from both, and the AC retargeted to the assertion message, naming the files that actually
hold the sites — plan_review_recovery.py (3) and plan_review/workflow_ops.py (2).

This is worth noting as a process point: the finding I got wrong was one I had asserted CONFIDENTLY
and repeated across three tickets and a session comment. The reviewer caught it by doing the one thing
I had not — reading the cited line. Editing file_impact and the description is safe here because the
attestation was BLOCK and therefore unsigned; nothing was destroyed.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
FRESH REVIEW: BLOCK, one finding, impact 1.0 — ACCEPTED, and I verified all three of its claims in
source before conceding.

FIRST, THE GOOD NEWS ON THE EARLIER ODDITY: the stale findings are GONE. This run returned 0
indeterminate, where the previous run reported findings quoting text that had already been removed.
So that was transient, and the decision NOT to re-edit in response to it was correct — re-editing
would have churned the description and invalidated the parent's pin for nothing. Leaving the note
rather than acting on it was the right call.

THE NEW FINDING IS A REAL DEFECT IN MY PLAN, not a nitpick. AC1 said the registry-membership test
must FAIL when the registration import at workflow_ops.py:45 is removed, and offered "prove it bites
by deleting the :45 import locally". That cannot work in a normal pytest run:
  * STEP_REGISTRY is a process-global dict — `STEP_REGISTRY: dict[str, ScriptedStep] = {}` at
    executor.py:155 — populated purely as an IMPORT SIDE EFFECT.
  * Python caches modules in sys.modules, so the registry is populated ONCE per process.
  * At least SIX test modules already import `rebar.llm.workflow.steps`, including
    tests/unit/workflow/test_contracts.py:16 (`from rebar.llm.workflow import steps  # noqa: F401 -
    registers the built-in contracts`), plus test_plan_review_triage.py,
    test_code_review_deletion_impact.py, test_audit_code_review_v2.py, test_code_review_nit_routing.py
    and test_code_review_project_criteria.py.
So by the time the new test runs, the registry is ALREADY full, and deleting the :45 import changes
nothing. The guard would pass whether or not the defect it exists to catch is present.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: this ticket's entire justification is that a missed registration
import is invisible to every existing layer (schema, linter, and test_contracts.py:186, which only
iterates what IS registered). Shipping a guard that is ITSELF unable to detect a missed registration
would reproduce the exact failure mode in the fix. A decorative guard is worse than none, because it
reads as coverage.

REMEDIATED: the membership assertion must run IN A SUBPROCESS with a clean sys.modules, using the
pattern the repo already has at tests/unit/test_structured_run_seam.py:115
(`subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], ...)`) — the only form that observes a first-import
registry. A second AC now requires recording that the same check run IN-PROCESS stays GREEN under the
same deletion: that contrast is the evidence the subprocess form is necessary rather than merely
tidier, and it stops a future reader from "simplifying" it back into the broken shape.

This is the second time on this ticket that the reviewer caught a claim I had asserted confidently
without executing. Both times the fix was to test the claim rather than to argue it.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
ROUND 3: BLOCK, two findings, both ACCEPTED. Neither is a nitpick and the second is my own
inconsistency introduced while fixing the first.

FINDING 1 — AC2 said the in-process blindness must be "recorded as evidence" and never named the
ARTIFACT. Fair: "recorded" with no location is unverifiable, and a completion verifier reading
repository files cannot confirm a claim that lives nowhere. Now specified concretely as two
artifacts: (a) the new test module's DOCSTRING must state that an in-process assertion stays green
when the workflow_ops.py:45 import is deleted and why the subprocess form is therefore mandatory —
that is the copy a future reader hits before "simplifying" it away; (b) a COMMENT ON THIS TICKET
quoting both observed outputs, the subprocess run reporting the missing op and the in-process run
passing, so the contrast is checkable rather than asserted.

FINDING 2 — AC3 HAD THE IDENTICAL DEFECT AND I LEFT IT. When I remediated AC1 to require subprocess
isolation, I did not carry the same requirement to AC3, even though the gate-YAML resolution test
reads the SAME process-global STEP_REGISTRY (executor.py:155). A pre-populated registry makes that
assertion pass regardless of whether the registration imports survive, so it too would be blind to
the defect it exists to catch. Fixed: AC3 now requires the same subprocess isolation and says
explicitly that sharing one helper between the two checks is preferred.

THE PATTERN WORTH NAMING, because it is the third instance on this ticket: each round I fixed the
specific thing the reviewer cited and did not sweep for OTHER instances of the same class. Round 2's
finding was "this assertion depends on a process-global pre-populated by imports"; the correct
response was to ask which OTHER assertions in the plan share that dependency, and AC3 obviously did.
Rather than wait for a round 4 to tell me, I swept the remaining criteria myself: AC4 is a pure LOC
read, AC5 is a text correction, AC6 is a no-op statement — none touches process-global state, so the
class is now fully covered by AC1-AC3.

Round 1 was a factual error (a docstring I called stale that was accurate). Round 2 was an
unexecutable falsification claim. Round 3 is an under-specified artifact plus a missed sibling. The
findings are getting narrower each round, which is convergence rather than thrash — but all three
share one cause: asserting something without running or sweeping for it.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
ROUND 4: BLOCK, one finding, ACCEPTED — and it is a trap I had ALREADY been burned by earlier in this session and reintroduced anyway.

AC2(b) required 'a comment on THIS ticket quotes both observed outputs'. A ticket comment lives OUTSIDE the repository, and the completion verifier reads repository files ONLY, so that criterion could never be confirmed from the codebase and would have burned a close cycle. This is the identical mechanism that blocked bug 7cbe's close a few hours ago, where the fix was to tag machine-local criteria [operator-attested]. I learned it there and then wrote the same shape back into this plan while remediating round 3.

REMEDIATED by splitting the criterion along the repo boundary rather than tagging the whole thing:
 - the DOCSTRING half stays untagged and in-repo. That is deliberate: the docstring is the artifact a future reader hits before 'simplifying' the subprocess isolation away, so it must live in the repository where the verifier — and the reader — can see it.
 - the EXPERIMENT half is now [operator-attested], because its evidence is transient command output with no repository artifact and no CI check.

APPLYING LAST ROUND'S LESSON RATHER THAN WAITING TO BE TOLD: I swept ALL criteria for out-of-repo evidence instead of fixing only the cited one. Result: AC3 is the only genuinely out-of-repo criterion and is now tagged. One apparent hit on the 'no production behaviour changes' criterion was a false positive of my own keyword heuristic — it matched the word 'comments' in 'corrects comments only', which is verifiable from the diff. Every other criterion asserts on a test or a repository file.

Round-by-round: (1) a factual error, (2) an unexecutable falsification claim, (3) an under-specified artifact plus a missed sibling, (4) an out-of-repo criterion. Narrowing each time. The recurring cause is asserting rather than checking, and the recurring fix is to run the sweep the finding implies instead of only the edit it names.

comments.body:
[operator-attested] THE EXPERIMENT WAS RUN. Both outputs below, verbatim. IMPLEMENTED AND PUSHED:
Gerrit change 1156, commit b9696dc8f.

PROCEDURE: delete the side-effect import at plan_review/workflow_ops.py:45
(`from . import prerequisite_workflow_ops as _prerequisite_workflow_ops`), then run the membership
check three ways. Restored afterwards; `git status` shows only the two intended test files.

  (1) IN-PROCESS, run ALONE:
        FAILED tests/unit/test_zz_inprocess_probe.py::test_inprocess_membership_probe
        AssertionError: IN-PROCESS DETECTED the missing op
        1 failed

  (2) IN-PROCESS, run AFTER tests/unit/test_plan_review_prerequisites_heldout.py:
        12 passed
        ^^ MASKED. The defect is present and the check is green.

  (3) THE SUBPROCESS GUARD, same conditions as (2):
        FAILED ...::test_every_plan_review_op_is_registered_on_a_first_import
        AssertionError: not registered on a first import: ['plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs']
        1 failed, 11 passed

I MUST CORRECT THE REVIEW FINDING I ACTED ON, because the conclusion was right for the wrong reason
and shipping the wrong reason in a docstring would mislead the next reader. The finding said the
in-process check is masked because "STEP_REGISTRY is a process-global and Python caches modules in
sys.modules — test_contracts.py:16 already imported rebar.llm.workflow.steps". Result (1) REFUTES
that: run alone, the in-process check FAILS. A source deletion is seen by every import in a fresh
process, so caching of `steps` masks nothing.

THE REAL MASKING PATH, found by grepping for other importers rather than reasoning:
tests/unit/test_plan_review_prerequisites_heldout.py:11 imports `prerequisite_workflow_ops` DIRECTLY.
That registers plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs regardless of whether the production import at
:45 survives — a TEST's convenience import silently substituting for the production one. Result (2)
demonstrates it.

WHY THAT IS WORSE THAN THE ORIGINAL DIAGNOSIS, and why the subprocess requirement stands: the
blindness is CONDITIONAL ON TEST ORDERING. The in-process guard would be green in a full CI run and
red when the file is run alone — or the reverse under `-p no:randomly` changes. A consistently blind
guard is at least consistently wrong; an order-dependent one produces contradictory evidence about
whether the codebase is healthy. The subprocess form is immune because it observes a FIRST import.

The shipped test module's docstring records this corrected mechanism, with all three measurements, so
the next reader who wants to "simplify" the subprocess away meets the evidence first. The ticket's own
Approach text still carries the original (caching) explanation; I did NOT edit it, because it is
material and the description's REQUIREMENT — subprocess isolation — is correct and unchanged, so a
re-edit would cost a review round to fix prose that the in-repo docstring already supersedes.

ALSO IN THIS CHANGE: test_gate_dispatch_seam.py's headroom assertion justified itself with "adding an
argument at its three finalize_verdict call sites". Ticket 1484 moved those out and gate_dispatch
holds ZERO; they live in plan_review_recovery.py (:223, :297, :336) and plan_review/workflow_ops.py
(2 sites). Corrected in both the docstring and the assertion message.

GATES: make lint clean (after rewrapping over-long docstring prose — ruff format does not reflow
docstrings), make typecheck clean, generator/parity gates clean, and 513 passed across
tests/unit/workflow plus both seam test files. No production code changed: the diff is two test files.

NOT CLOSING until 1156 is Verified +1.

compiled_state.description:
# Seam guards: step-registry membership, gate-YAML resolution, and headroom for the unguarded hot files

## Context / Problem
With the per-FUNCTION ratchet declined by the operator (blast radius: 62 functions over 120 lines
across six subsystems), SEAM TESTS are the only remaining structural defence against module regrowth.
Change 1484 added `< 700` headroom assertions for `gate_dispatch.py` and `orchestrator.py`, and those
two are the comfortable files today BECAUSE of it. The files that hurt now have no such guard.

THREE CONCRETE GAPS, all verified in the tree:

**1. No headroom guard on the files that need it.** `tests/unit/test_gate_dispatch_seam.py:26-29`
pins exactly four paths — `gate_dispatch.py`, `plan_review_recovery.py`, `orchestrator.py`,
`context_assembly.py`. `plan_review/workflow_ops.py` (794 LOC) and `llm/config.py` (793) appear
NOWHERE. `tests/unit/test_structured_run_seam.py:31-33` does the same for `runner.py` only.

**2. A guard whose stated premise is STALE.**
`test_gate_dispatch_seam.py:46-53` asserts `gate_dispatch.py < 700` and justifies itself with
"adding an argument at its three finalize_verdict call sites is not a build break" (`:52`). Change
1484 MOVED those three sites to `workflow/plan_review_recovery.py`. VERIFIED: the five
`finalize_verdict` sites are now `plan_review/workflow_ops.py:223` and `:760`, and
`plan_review_recovery.py:223`, `:297`, `:336` — ZERO remain in `gate_dispatch.py`. The assertion still
passes (527 LOC) but guards a premise that no longer holds, and the two sites that DO need protection
sit in the unguarded file. The prose at `:4` and at `plan_review_recovery.py:8` is stale the same way.

**3. An unregistered workflow step cannot be caught statically — the worst of the three.**
`@register_step` writes into the process-global `STEP_REGISTRY` as an IMPORT SIDE EFFECT
(`workflow/executor.py:180`, assignment at `:203`). Registration depends on a single import chain:
`workflow/steps.py:341` imports `plan_review.workflow_ops`, which at `:45` imports
`prerequisite_workflow_ops` purely for its side effect. Nothing asserts either import survives — a
routine "remove unused import" cleanup would silently unregister
`plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs`. THIS HAZARD IS ALREADY LATENT TODAY, before any refactor.
And no layer catches it:
 * the workflow schema treats `uses` as a free-form string (`workflow/schema.py:331`, `:372`);
 * `lint_workflow` treats an unknown step as UNKNOWN and SKIPS validation BY DESIGN
   (`workflow/lint_refs.py:441-447`, `executor.py:214-216`), so the lint-clean test still passes;
 * `tests/unit/workflow/test_contracts.py:186` LOOKS like a completeness guard but iterates
   `STEP_REGISTRY` itself — an op that vanished from the registry is invisible to it.
Only a runtime `WorkflowError` (`executor.py:676`) catches it, and only for ops on an executed path.

## Approach
Add the guards, and land this BEFORE any relocation so the guards exist independently of the refactor
they protect — the refactor must not be the change that also introduces its own safety net.

THE THRESHOLD IS STAGED, and an earlier draft of this plan contradicted itself on it (Approach said
`< 700`, Testing said `< 800`) — resolved here in favour of staging, because the two files this guard
covers are ABOVE 700 TODAY (`workflow_ops.py` 794, `config.py` 793). A `< 700` assertion would land
RED, so this ticket asserts `< 800` (the hard cap — still a real guard: it catches the next commit
that would breach) and the sibling EXTRACTION tickets tighten their own file to `< 700` in the same
change that creates the headroom. That keeps every ticket independently landable.

`< 700` remains the POLICY number the extractions must reach, and it is calibrated rather than
arbitrary: it matches both existing seam tests, and 100 lines of headroom absorbs observed change
size — median per-commit delta to `workflow_ops.py` over its last 20 commits ~+10, mean ~+18,
p90 ~+45, worst +185 (`f373cf4a6e`). Do NOT assert tighter than 700 even after the extraction:
encoding a refactor's OUTCOME turns the guard into a change-detector that fails on the next
legitimate commit while saying nothing about correctness.

## Scope
- `tests/unit/` — a new plan-review workflow-ops seam test; the registry-membership and
  gate-YAML-resolution guards.
- `tests/unit/test_gate_dispatch_seam.py` — correct the stale rationale to name the file that now holds
  the call sites.
  (`plan_review_recovery.py` is deliberately NOT in scope — its docstring was verified accurate.)

## Testing
- assert the exact expected plan-review step-registry membership: the eight ops in `workflow_ops`
  plus `plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs`.
  **THE ASSERTION MUST RUN IN A SUBPROCESS WITH A CLEAN `sys.modules`.** An in-process check cannot
  be falsified and would be a decorative guard: `STEP_REGISTRY` is a process-global dict
  (`executor.py:155`) populated as an IMPORT SIDE EFFECT, and at least six test modules already
  import `rebar.llm.workflow.steps` — `tests/unit/workflow/test_contracts.py:16` among them. So in
  any normal pytest run the registry is ALREADY populated before this test executes, and deleting
  the registration import at `workflow_ops.py:45` would NOT turn it red. Use the subprocess pattern
  the repo already has at `tests/unit/test_structured_run_seam.py:115`
  (`subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], ...)`), which is the only form that observes a
  first-import registry.
- PROVE IT BITES, and prove it in the subprocess form: with the `:45` import removed, the check must
  report `plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs` missing. An in-process run of the same check stays
  green under that deletion — that contrast IS the evidence the subprocess form is required, so
  record both observations rather than only the red one.
- assert every `uses:` in `gates/plan-review.yaml` resolves in `STEP_REGISTRY`. Location-independent by
  construction, so it survives every future move — `plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs` already
  lives in another module while referenced at `plan-review.yaml:136`, which is the working proof.
- headroom assertions for `plan_review/workflow_ops.py` and `llm/config.py`. These will pass only
  AFTER their sibling extraction tickets land, so this ticket asserts the weak `< 800` form now and the
  extraction tickets tighten to `< 700` — otherwise this ticket lands red.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] a test asserts the full expected plan-review step-registry membership FROM A SUBPROCESS with a
      clean `sys.modules`, and it FAILS when the registration import at `workflow_ops.py:45` is
      removed. The subprocess is load-bearing, not stylistic: `STEP_REGISTRY` is a process-global
      populated at import time and six-plus test modules already import `rebar.llm.workflow.steps`,
      so an in-process assertion stays GREEN under that deletion and would be a guard that cannot
      detect the very defect it exists for
- [ ] IN-REPO, and therefore verifiable from the codebase alone: the new test module's docstring
      states that an in-process assertion stays GREEN when the `workflow_ops.py:45` import is
      deleted, and why the subprocess form is consequently mandatory. This is the artifact a future
      reader hits before "simplifying" the subprocess away, so it must live in the repository rather
      than in a ticket
- [ ] [operator-attested] the experiment behind that docstring is actually RUN and its two outputs
      recorded on this ticket — the subprocess check reporting `plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs`
      missing, and the in-process check passing under the same deletion. Tagged because the evidence
      is a transient command output with no repository artifact and no CI check: the completion
      verifier reads repository files ONLY, so an untagged criterion of this shape cannot be
      confirmed and burns a close cycle
- [ ] a test asserts every `uses:` in `gates/plan-review.yaml` is present in `STEP_REGISTRY`,
      RUN IN THE SAME SUBPROCESS ISOLATION as the membership check above. This is the identical
      defect, not a stylistic echo: this assertion reads the same process-global `STEP_REGISTRY`
      (`executor.py:155`), so a pre-populated registry makes it pass regardless of whether the
      registration imports survive — it too would be blind to the defect it exists to catch.
      Sharing one subprocess helper between the two checks is fine and preferred
- [ ] a test asserts a headroom bound for `plan_review/workflow_ops.py` and for `llm/config.py`,
      at `< 800` — the staged form, since both exceed 700 until their extraction tickets land
- [ ] `test_gate_dispatch_seam.py`'s assertion message no longer claims `gate_dispatch.py` holds
      `finalize_verdict` call sites (it holds zero); it names the files that do —
      `plan_review_recovery.py` (3) and `plan_review/workflow_ops.py` (2)
- [ ] no production behaviour changes: this ticket adds tests and corrects comments only

file_impact.reason: correct the stale assertion message naming gate_dispatch as holding the call sites
new seam test: registry membership, gate-YAML resolution, staged headroom guards
